 ## Search results
NextItNet’s residual dilated causal convolutions provide an efficient backbone for expanding historical context, but do not themselves establish which older interactions remain relevant to current intent. The closest recent convolutional result found was TV-Rec: position-dependent, time-variant filters replace fixed kernels and self-attention to capture changing interaction patterns. This supports investigating adaptive convolutional weighting, although it does not establish that a time-decayed NextItNet improves this benchmark. Sources: [NextItNet](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf), [TV-Rec](https://openreview.net/pdf/e9c3bd1680a3ab54ffe119fc526e57d9835d7b8d.pdf).

Practical hypothesis: retain NextItNet residual causal blocks and jointly learn gates over convolutional features at different dilation depths, allowing each position to emphasize shorter or longer context within one network. Add a nonnegative learned decay conditioned on log elapsed time, using only timestamps observable in each training prefix. A 2026 temporal-prior paper explicitly measures recency relative to the latest observed interaction, avoiding target-timestamp leakage; its decay coefficient is validation-selected, so learned decay remains a proposed extension. Compare adaptive gates and decay through validation ablations rather than assuming stale history is harmful. Preserve padding masks, final nonpadding readout, and one checkpoint per category; keep timestamp handling and architecture identical in training and the predictor writer. Source: [Interaction-Specific Diffusion Scheduling Guided by Temporal Priors](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/15/19/4389).

---

Recent work supports combining item text with interaction signals, but provides limited direct evidence for a scratch-trained, content-aware NextItNet. [Sequence-level Semantic Representation Fusion (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18166) argues that text and ID features have different characteristics, making simple addition less effective. [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/9/1748) combines IDs with titles, descriptions and reviews, but uses pretrained BERT and unavailable review data. [WhitenRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10602) identifies excessive similarity among pretrained text embeddings as an obstacle to distinguishing items; its pretrained features and ensemble variant are unsuitable here, although representation collapse is a useful diagnostic concern.

A constraint-compatible hypothesis is one NextItNet with randomly initialized token embeddings, pooled title/description features, and a jointly learned gate combining text with item IDs. Train everything through the next-item objective; compare against the corrected ID-only baseline using macro validation HR@10. This is an architectural proposal, not an established result from those papers. Text similarity alone cannot establish functional compatibility: [Function-based labels for complementary recommendation](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167865525003976) explicitly studies functional relationship labels, while [complementary-product research (2024)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/13/23/4851) cautions that co-purchase can misleadingly imply complementarity. With only histories, titles and descriptions, treat purchase intent, complements and substitutes as latent hypotheses; avoid invented relationship labels or separately fitted scoring components.

---

Recent work supports testing multi-negative sampled softmax while retaining NextItNet’s causal dilated-convolution backbone. [Wu et al., 2024](https://wujcan.github.io/papers/tois-ssm.pdf) show that temperature controls emphasis on hard negatives; excessively low temperature lets a few difficult examples dominate gradients. [Scalable Cross-Entropy, RecSys 2024](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/5392aca9-0bae-4176-9b3a-a8165957ba26) approximates catalog-wide cross-entropy by selecting informative outputs. [Correcting the LogQ Correction, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331) distinguishes deterministically included positives from sampled negatives when correcting sampling bias. This correction addresses the sampling distribution, not false-negative identification.

Hardness needs controls: [AHNS, AAAI 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05191) motivates adapting negative difficulty rather than always selecting the hardest items, although its experiments concern collaborative filtering. [Sequential sampling experiments, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) find substantial head/mid/tail trade-offs: uniform negatives favor head items, while popularity-based sampling can improve balance at an overall accuracy cost. These results do not establish gains for Electronics or this evaluator.
